title: Understanding HA Fencing Loops
text:
A fencing loop occurs when the Proxmox HA Manager repeatedly fences (forcibly powers off) the same node within a short window — typically because the node is rebooting faster than the fence timeout, or because the root cause (IPMI unreachability, storage I/O hang, NIC flap) is never cleared between fence attempts.
The VM workload migrates to surviving nodes, runs briefly, then gets fenced again when the problem node rejoins and the same condition recurs. This produces continuous failover churn and can saturate surviving nodes.

title: Understanding HA Fencing Loops
text:
2 The Architecture of HA Fencing
Proxmox HA uses a watchdog/fencing mechanism to enforce node isolation before recovering VMs. The sequence below shows the normal flow and where a loop forms.


Code
sequenceDiagram
    participant HA as HA Manager
    participant Node as Faulted Node
    participant IPMI as IPMI / Fence Agent
    participant Cluster as Surviving Nodes

    HA->>Node: Heartbeat lost
    HA->>IPMI: Fence node (power off)
    IPMI-->>HA: Fenced OK
    HA->>Cluster: Recover VMs from fenced node
    Note over Node,HA: Node reboots and rejoins...
    Node-->>HA: Heartbeat restored
    HA->>Node: Heartbeat lost (condition recurs!)
    HA->>IPMI: Fence node AGAIN ← loop begins





sequenceDiagram
    participant HA as HA Manager
    participant Node as Faulted Node
    participant IPMI as IPMI / Fence Agent
    participant Cluster as Surviving Nodes

    HA->>Node: Heartbeat lost
    HA->>IPMI: Fence node (power off)
    IPMI-->>HA: Fenced OK
    HA->>Cluster: Recover VMs from fenced node
    Note over Node,HA: Node reboots and rejoins...
    Node-->>HA: Heartbeat restored
    HA->>Node: Heartbeat lost (condition recurs!)
    HA->>IPMI: Fence node AGAIN ← loop begins

title: Understanding HA Fencing Loops
text:
3 Why Loops Are Dangerous







Risk
Explanation




VM churn
VMs are migrated and killed in rapid succession, causing application-layer disruption


Surviving node overload
Each failover wave lands workload on remaining nodes; repeated waves compound load


Storage state corruption
Repeated unclean shutdowns can invalidate QCOW2 dirty bitmaps or RBD journal entries


Quorum degradation
If two nodes loop-fence simultaneously, the cluster may lose quorum entirely

title: Understanding HA Fencing Loops
text:
4 The Safety Guardrail
library/pve_ha.py introduces detect_ha_fencing_loop, which scans the Proxmox task history for completed hamanager fence events within a configurable observation window.


Code
# Core detection logic
tasks = proxmox.nodes(node).tasks.get()
fence_events = [
    t for t in tasks
    if t["type"] == "hamanager" and "fence" in t["id"] and t["status"] != "running"
]

# Group by fenced node and count within the window
for node, events in events_by_node.items():
    if len(events) >= threshold:
        report.looping_nodes.append(node)


The function returns a FencingLoopReport with an is_safe boolean. Runbook steps and any automation that modifies HA state must gate on report.is_safe.

flowchart TD

    B -- No --> C[🚨 Escalate — split-brain protocol]

title: Understanding HA Fencing Loops
text:
6 Common Root Causes
IPMI / BMC unreachability — The fence agent confirms the fence but the node boots again before the issue is resolved. Check BMC firmware and network path to the management VLAN.
Storage I/O hang — A Ceph or NFS I/O stall causes the node’s watchdog to expire repeatedly. Look for hung_task kernel messages in journalctl on the affected node.
NIC / bond flap — Loss of the cluster network causes heartbeat failure. The node fences, reboots, rejoins, and loses the cluster network again. Check dmesg for link-down events and inspect switch port counters.
Misconfigured fence timeout — A fence timeout shorter than the node’s POST/boot time means the node is guaranteed to rejoin before it is considered truly isolated.

title: Understanding & Fixing locked: backup
text:
When a Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) backup is interrupted (usually via network timeout), the Proxmox hypervisor may fail to drop the backup lock on the VM configuration file (/etc/pve/qemu-server/<vmid>.conf).
The VM will remain running, but SREs cannot migrate, resize, or reboot the VM until the lock is cleared. That behavior protects against the corruption of the QEMU dirty-bitmap tracking used for incremental backups.

title: Understanding & Fixing locked: backup
text:
2 The Architecture of a Lock
When vzdump runs, it manipulates the QEMU process to track “dirty” blocks.


Code
sequenceDiagram
    participant PBS as Proxmox Backup Server
    participant PVE as PVE Node
    participant QEMU as VM Process

    PBS->>PVE: Request Backup (API)
    PVE->>PVE: Write `lock: backup` to config
    PVE->>QEMU: Initiate Snapshot / Dirty Bitmap
    QEMU-->>PVE: Stream data
    PVE-->>PBS: Send Chunks
    Note over PBS,PVE: If network drops here, lock remains!





sequenceDiagram
    participant PBS as Proxmox Backup Server
    participant PVE as PVE Node
    participant QEMU as VM Process

    PBS->>PVE: Request Backup (API)
    PVE->>PVE: Write `lock: backup` to config
    PVE->>QEMU: Initiate Snapshot / Dirty Bitmap
    QEMU-->>PVE: Stream data
    PVE-->>PBS: Send Chunks
    Note over PBS,PVE: If network drops here, lock remains!

3 Remediation Protocol
Do not use the GUI to blindly unlock the VM. Follow the interactive runbook below.

title: Understanding & Fixing locked: backup
section: 4 Under the Hood: The Safety Guardrail
text:
4 Under the Hood: The Safety Guardrail
Our library/pve_safety.py module queries the /api2/json/nodes/{node}/tasks endpoint. If any task matches type: vzdump and the vmid, we block the unlock command to prevent corrupting the QCOW2/RBD image.


Code
# Core safety logic abstraction
tasks = proxmox.nodes(node).tasks.get()
for task in tasks:
    if task['status'] == 'running' and task['type'] == 'vzdump':
        raise Exception("Unsafe to unlock!")

title: Incident Review: HA Fencing Loop
text:
2 Incident Log

2.1 INC-002 — 2025-05-20







Field
Detail




Node
pve-node-03


Fence events in window
5 (detected within 47 minutes)


Root cause
IPMI BMC unreachable from fence agent due to management VLAN misconfiguration after a switch firmware upgrade


Impact
8 VMs migrated repeatedly across pve-node-01 and pve-node-02; two VMs experienced application-layer errors due to rapid successive restarts


Resolved by
Node isolated via maintenance mode; VLAN ACL corrected; node re-added after BMC reachability confirmed


Resolution time
1 hour 12 minutes


Runbook followed
Yes — ha_fencing_loop.md


Safety check passed
Yes — detect_ha_fencing_loop confirmed loop before intervention; quorum verified intact (2 of 3 nodes)



Timeline:

03:41 — Switch firmware upgrade completes on mgmt switch; management VLAN ACL silently drops IPMI traffic
03:44 — HA Manager loses heartbeat on pve-node-03; issues first fence via IPMI
03:44 — Fence “succeeds” (IPMI unreachable → agent times out with success assumption); node reboots unassisted
03:49 — pve-node-03 rejoins cluster; heartbeat re-established briefly
03:51 — Heartbeat lost again (node NIC negotiation delay post-boot); second fence issued
04:11 — On-call SRE paged: 4 fence events in 30 minutes
04:18 — detect_ha_fencing_loop confirms loop; quorum verified at 2/3
04:22 — pve-node-03 placed in maintenance mode; fencing stops
04:38 — Management VLAN ACL corrected; IPMI reachability verified from fence agent
04:53 — pve-node-03 removed from maintenance; HA resources re-enabled; cluster stable

Notes: > The fence agent was configured to treat IPMI timeout as a successful fence (default Proxmox behaviour). This is intentional — an unreachable BMC is assumed to mean the node is powered off. The real fix is ensuring BMC reachability before production changes to the management network. A pre-change checklist item has been added.

title: Incident Review: HA Fencing Loop
text:
3 Recurring Patterns

All recorded loop events have involved pve-node-03 — its BMC is on a separate management VLAN that has been involved in two separate network changes
Loop duration before detection: average 27 minutes — detection alerting threshold to be reduced to 10 minutes (2 fence events)
No data corruption observed in any incident; RBD journals recovered cleanly in all cases
